expert_opinion.quote:
Thus our procedure
represents a close (near exact in Study 3) replication of
the equivalent studies by Critcher and Gilovich (2008),

Dogerlioglu-Demir and Koçaş (2015), and Koçaş and
Dogerlioglu-Demir (2020) but nevertheless failed to
detect an incidental anchoring effect.
expert_opinion.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In Studies 1-3, Shanks et al. (2020) empirically test whether incidental environmental anchors in marketing communications and consumer scenarios bias price and willingness-to-pay estimations, and the General Discussion explicitly concludes that their procedure is a close replication of the equivalent studies by Critcher and Gilovich (2008), Dogerlioglu-Demir and Koçaş (2015), and Koçaş and Dogerlioglu-Demir (2020) that failed to detect an incidental anchoring effect. The reference list (p. 14) identifies this target as Koçaş, C., & Dogerlioglu-Demir, K. (2020), 'The 1 in 1,000,000: Context effects of how numbers cue different kinds of incidental environmental anchoring in marketing communications,' Journal of Business Research, 109, 536-544, DOI 10.1016/j.jbusres.2019.01.027 (confirmed in Crossref metadata). Luna's triage mistakenly conflated this 2020 Journal of Business Research article with shipped row 1494; in fact, shipped row 1475 is Critcher and Gilovich (2007/2008, DOI 10.1002/bdm.586, sibling target 0) and shipped row 1494 is the earlier Marketing Letters article by Dogerlioglu-Demir and Koçaş (2014/2015, 'Seemingly incidental anchoring: the effect of incidental environmental anchors on consumers’ willingness to pay,' DOI 10.1007/s11002-014-9295-0, sibling target 1). Both the main text and Note 1 distinguish the 2015 Marketing Letters study from the 2020 Journal of Business Research study, establishing that target 2 is a separate original work genuinely absent from all shipped rows.

source_evidence.quote:
In their remaining experiments (Studies 2–4),
Dogerlioglu-Demir and Koçaş (2015) elicited
willingness-to-pay estimates for hamburger meal
advertisements as a function of the product’s name
(e.g., ‘the 1999 burger’). Because participants tended
to interpret the numbers as associated with price,
these are not truly incidental in the way that a number
on a sportsman’s jersey is incidental. The studies in
Koçaş and Dogerlioglu-Demir (2020) explored ways in
which ambiguous anchor values (e.g., negative values)
are interpreted.

source_evidence.quote:
Study 1 aims to replicate the design of Study 3 by Critcher
and Gilovich (2008) and Study 1 by Dogerlioglu-Demir
and Koçaş (2015), asking participants to report their
willingness to pay for a meal at a restaurant described as
either Studio 97 or Studio 17. In addition to the restaurant
item, participants gave price estimations for 6 other
goods and services, including technology items similar to
those used in Critcher and Gilovich’s Study 2. Based on
their findings, we expect all high anchor items to produce
higher price estimations than the low anchor items.

expert_opinion.quote:
The two
final standard anchoring trials were added to the survey
flow after all the incidental trials. These items enabled a
replication of the classic anchoring procedure designed by
Tversky and Kahneman (1974).
expert_opinion.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In Studies 2 and 3, the authors empirically administer standard comparative-plus-estimation anchoring trials alongside incidental anchoring items, explicitly stating in Study 2 Method (p. 6) that these items enabled a replication of the classic anchoring procedure designed by Tversky and Kahneman (1974) and reporting robust anchoring effects in the Results of Studies 2 and 3 (pp. 6, 8) and the Meta-Analysis (pp. 9-10). The reference list (p. 15) and Crossref metadata identify the original as Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974), 'Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases,' Science, 185, 1124-1131, DOI 10.1126/science.185.4157.1124. This classic standard anchoring paper is completely distinct from shipped rows 1475 (Critcher & Gilovich, 2007/2008, DOI 10.1002/bdm.586) and 1494 (Dogerlioglu-Demir & Koçaş, 2014/2015, DOI 10.1007/s11002-014-9295-0) as well as sibling target 2 (Koçaş & Dogerlioglu-Demir, 2020, DOI 10.1016/j.jbusres.2019.01.027), all of which test incidental environmental anchoring.

source_evidence.quote:
In a prototypical or standard anchoring
demonstration reported by Tversky and Kahneman (1974),
participants generated what appeared to be an arbitrary
number from 0–100 by spinning a roulette wheel. In
fact, the wheel was rigged to generate either a low (10)
or a high (65) ‘anchor’ number. Next, they were asked to
estimate whether the percentage of African nations in the
United Nations was lower or higher than that number.
